There is no such thing as ai.

I know that AI researchers usually have nothing more than a tired laugh for media that humanizes artificial intelligence, but I'm still curious as to how far its creation by humans engineers would reflect on the though process of an actual AI, should one be developed at some point in the future.

My completely unfounded guess is that we run the risk of creating intelligent machines that suffer from our failings when we work too hard to make them able to understand and communicate with us. We can't give them those abilities without making them think like us to some degree.

Unfortunately, machines that can communicate and serve us like our fellow humans are a big part of our ultimate goals in AI.

Most of the things we think of as "human" are actually pretty reasonable heuristics for dealing with the real world. It'd be crazy not to expect some of them to show up in AIs.

  • System shouldn't repeat itself too often or it could get stuck in a loop: Boredom.
  • System should anticipate dangers and take steps to protect itself: Fear/anger.
  • System should gather new information when possible to increase its knowledge base: Curiosity.
  • System should monitor its power supply and recharge as necessary: Hunger.
  • System should remember past mistakes and losses and try to avoid repeats: Sadness.
  • System should be able to work cooperatively with a group of similar systems: Communication, compassion, negotiation, politics.

Given that most of these thought processes can be linked back to basic self-preservation instincts, I think this is fairly reasonable. But if you look back at Rossum's Universal Robots (the first work of fiction that actually used the term "robot"), one might start to worry that a man-made AI would also inherent man's flaws - violent means to reach its ends, the constant hunger for additional resources, etc., etc.
So maybe 'robot personalities' would develop after AI systems start prioritizing those traits, or start making strategies based on them.
